articles.title: Understand elevation profiles on a planned walk
articles.summary: Use ascent and descent information as planning context rather than a promise of route difficulty.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Start, High point, Finish. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Read the profile alongside the route
paragraphs: An elevation profile summarises how mapped height changes along a planned route. Look for the overall shape, sustained rises and descents, and where they appear relative to landmarks or planned stops.
A profile is an interpretation of map data, not a view of the actual ground. Its accuracy depends on the mapping source, route alignment and how closely elevation samples represent the path.

sections.title: Avoid false precision
paragraphs: Check whether the vertical and horizontal scales differ. A steep-looking line may be exaggerated by the display, and a short profile can hide uneven surfaces or steps.
Record notable height changes as planning considerations, not guarantees of speed, accessibility or safety. Weather, fatigue and terrain can make an apparently modest change more demanding.

sections.title: Keep context with offline copies
paragraphs: Save the map area and the route notes alongside any profile image or numbers. Include the source and date so an old screenshot is not mistaken for a current route assessment.
If the profile conflicts with local signs, path closures or actual conditions, do not treat the profile as authority. Reassess the plan using current reliable information before proceeding.

articles.title: Recognise common contour patterns on walking maps
articles.summary: Learn what closely spaced, widely spaced and closed contour lines represent.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Spacing, Shape, Legend. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Read the map's contour legend
paragraphs: Contour lines connect points of equal mapped elevation. The legend or marginal information explains the interval between adjacent lines, which varies by map product.
A series of close lines usually indicates more rapid height change across a shorter map distance; widely spaced lines suggest gentler mapped gradients. Neither pattern alone establishes safe footing.

sections.title: Interpret shapes cautiously
paragraphs: Closed contours can indicate a hill or depression depending on map symbols and height labels. Valleys and ridges create bending patterns that are easier to understand with labelled heights and nearby features.
Avoid assuming a contour pattern reveals cliffs, obstacles, vegetation or route accessibility. Those may require other symbols, recent mapping or on-site information.

sections.title: Compare with a real route
paragraphs: Use contour patterns as one input when comparing possible routes, alongside path status, mapped surfaces, forecast conditions and the abilities of the group.
If the contour interval or symbols are unclear, keep the uncertainty visible in route notes rather than presenting a precise gradient or difficulty rating.

articles.title: Check an offline mapping app before leaving connectivity
articles.summary: Confirm saved map tiles, device settings and app access while still online.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Download, Open offline, Check area. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Confirm what was actually saved
paragraphs: A saved route line is not necessarily the same as downloaded map imagery. Inspect the app's offline-area settings and ensure the map includes the full planned route and reasonable surrounding context.
Check the map's scale, labels and geographic coverage while connected. Some apps limit offline access, require sign-in periodically or store different map layers separately.

sections.title: Test without a connection
paragraphs: Before departure, temporarily disable network access and reopen the app and downloaded area. Confirm the route, legend and essential notes remain accessible without fetching new data.
A device may still determine a location without mobile data, but location performance and battery use vary. An offline map does not provide live closures, forecasts or emergency communications.

sections.title: Prepare a fallback
paragraphs: Keep essential meeting information and route notes independently accessible, and consider a suitable paper map where appropriate. Check battery condition and access permissions.
Record when the map was downloaded. If the app fails the offline test, resolve the issue before relying on it rather than assuming the download completed.

articles.title: Check whether map symbols are readable for your group
articles.summary: Assess labels, contrast and alternative descriptions in offline route materials.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Contrast, Labels, Backup. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Check symbols at the size actually used
paragraphs: Open the saved map at a comfortable zoom level on the intended device. Verify that paths, water features, boundaries and warnings are distinguishable without relying solely on colour.
Compare similarly shaped symbols against the map's own legend. A symbol can change meaning between map publishers, and colour differences may be hard to see in glare or low light.

sections.title: Support different reading needs
paragraphs: Use short written notes for important symbols and decision points, especially where a small icon could be confused with another. Avoid relying on an unexplained abbreviation or a colour-only key.

Where possible, test the map with enlarged system text, screen magnification and any assistive technology the group uses. A static screenshot may not support text reflow or screen-reader interpretation.

sections.title: Keep alternative information available
paragraphs: Save a plain-language route summary that names key locations and uncertainties without duplicating an entire map. This can help if a printed copy becomes damaged or a display is difficult to read.
Accessibility is specific to the person and route. Ask what format works before travel and do not treat an automated accessibility score as a guarantee of usable terrain.

articles.title: Record practical facilities at a walking route start
articles.summary: Keep a simple offline record of access, facilities and their verification status.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Locate, Verify, Record. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Identify facilities that matter
paragraphs: For the planned starting point, list relevant facilities such as public transport connections, toilets, water access, accessible entrances or permitted parking. Separate essential needs from conveniences.
A map icon or old review does not establish that a facility is operating, accessible or free to use today. Note where information came from and whether it was confirmed by the operator.

sections.title: Record useful details without overcollection
paragraphs: Write down an understandable location description, an official contact or information source where available, and any published restrictions that matter to the group.
Avoid storing unnecessary personal information about staff or visitors. A public car park or toilet may have seasonal opening arrangements, closures or access requirements.

sections.title: Prepare for changes
paragraphs: Check facilities close to departure and consider reasonable alternatives for essential needs. Keep an offline copy of the route start and transport information.
If a facility is unexpectedly unavailable, reassess the plan rather than relying on a generic statement that services should be present.

articles.title: Organise spare clothing layers for a day walk
articles.summary: Keep dry spare layers accessible without assuming one packing list suits every condition.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Quick access, Dry spare, After use. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Choose layers for the actual plan
paragraphs: Review the expected conditions, duration, exertion and personal comfort needs. A spare insulating or weather-resistant layer may be useful, but no universal number of garments suits every route or person.
Check garment condition and fit before packing. Different fabrics behave differently when wet, and a garment's marketing label does not guarantee warmth or waterproofness.

sections.title: Arrange the bag for access
paragraphs: Keep frequently needed clothing reachable without unpacking everything. Protect spare dry items using suitable internal storage and separate damp items where practical.
Avoid overfilling the bag or placing heavy equipment where it creates discomfort or instability. If several people share equipment, agree who carries what and how it can be located.

sections.title: Review after returning
paragraphs: Air and dry used layers according to their care labels, and check for damage before storage. Note anything that was difficult to find or unnecessary on the trip.
Treat the packing layout as a reusable reminder rather than a safety certification. Adjust it to changing forecasts, accessibility needs and personal circumstances.

articles.title: Check route access permissions before a walk
articles.summary: Distinguish mapped paths from permission to enter or use land.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Map source, Access rules, Recheck. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Distinguish a route line from a right of access
paragraphs: A mapped trail, GPS track or user-shared route does not by itself establish a legal right to walk, cycle or camp there. Rules differ by jurisdiction, land type and activity.
Look for official access information and relevant route designations. A publicly visible path may still have temporary restrictions, and an informal track may cross private or sensitive land.

sections.title: Check conditions that can change
paragraphs: Review official notices for temporary closures, seasonal restrictions or conservation requirements where relevant. Record the information source and date rather than treating an old screenshot as permanent permission.
Where a sign conflicts with an older app route, do not assume the app is correct. Seek reliable local guidance before entering restricted or uncertain areas.

sections.title: Share a clear, respectful plan
paragraphs: Explain any access uncertainty to the group and choose a lawful alternative when permission cannot be established. Keep gates, livestock and sensitive habitats in mind without inventing universal rules.
The article is an informational planning checklist, not legal advice. Verify local law and official access guidance for the specific place and activity.

articles.title: Check time and coordinate settings on navigation devices
articles.summary: Identify settings mismatches that can make saved navigation notes confusing.

visual.alt: An offline schematic with 3 labelled elements: Time, Coordinates, Units. It is a planning aid, not a depiction of actual terrain or current conditions.
visual.caption: Conceptual planning illustration; check the full guide and local information.

sections.title: Compare time displays
paragraphs: Check that the device time and date make sense before relying on time-stamped notes. Devices may show local time, UTC or a manually selected time zone, and daylight-saving changes can create confusion.
When sharing route notes, state which time convention was used. A timestamp without a time zone can be misread even when the recorded time was accurate.

sections.title: Check coordinate formats and units
paragraphs: Confirm whether a saved location uses latitude and longitude, a national grid reference or another coordinate system. Note the map datum or grid system when provided rather than silently converting between formats.
Two coordinate strings can refer to different positions if their formats or reference systems differ. Copy labels exactly and verify with the intended map before using them for planning.

sections.title: Keep the settings record simple
paragraphs: Record the device or app, coordinate format, distance units and time convention with shared offline notes. Recheck after software updates, device replacement or restoring a backup.
This is a data-consistency check, not a substitute for navigation training or an assurance of location accuracy.
